A0022.title: Traffic Encryption
A0022.definition: Encrypting network request traffic or response traffic.
A0022.description: Traffic encryption typically provides a protection mechanism for process security. By encrypting data during transmission, attackers cannot directly obtain the original data or directly modify it.
A0022.limitation: Traffic encryption increases the complexity and cost of data transmission. When using traffic encryption, the trade-off between security and performance impact needs to be considered.

A0022-001.title: Transport Protocol Encryption
A0022-001.definition: Encrypting the entire transport layer or application layer communication data using custom algorithms or modified standard encryption algorithms.
A0022-001.description: Transport layer encryption refers to encrypting data at the transport layer to prevent interception or tampering during transmission, such as by modifying SSL/TLS. Application layer encryption refers to encrypting data at the application layer to prevent interception or tampering during transmission, such as by modifying HTTPS. Because the data transmission protocol itself is directly encrypted, it can ignore the specific upper-layer business scenarios and achieve full coverage of all business scenarios under the application.
A0022-001.limitation: Not applicable to scenarios where a browser is used for web page access. Additionally, modified protocols can still be cracked and reversed by attackers through packet capture tools, hooking remote request functions, or protocol-layer reverse engineering. Once the custom encryption algorithm is reversed, all traffic encryption protection can be bypassed.

A0022-002.title: Request Data Encryption
A0022-002.definition: Encrypting request data sent to the server to prevent interception or tampering during transmission.
A0022-002.description: Request data encryption refers to encrypting the request body on top of an existing protocol (such as HTTPS) before sending it to the server, to ensure data is not stolen or tampered with during transmission. Request data encryption can be applied in any business scenario, but requires decryption logic to be added on the server side.
A0022-002.limitation: Generally implemented by hooking the remote request function to encrypt data, but this may cause certain compatibility issues. If some business logic does not use a unified remote request function, that portion of data cannot be encrypted.

A0022-003.title: Response Data Encryption
A0022-003.definition: Encrypting response data from the server to prevent interception or tampering during transmission.
A0022-003.description: Response data encryption refers to encrypting the response body on the server side to ensure data is not stolen or tampered with during transmission. Response data encryption can be applied in any business scenario, but requires decryption logic to be added on the client side.
A0022-003.limitation: Generally implemented by hooking the remote request function to encrypt data, but this may cause certain compatibility issues. If some business logic does not use a unified remote request function, that portion of data cannot be encrypted.

A0022-004.title: Custom Transport Protocol
A0022-004.definition: A non-standard communication protocol, self-developed or derived from modifying a standard protocol at the transport or application layer, that prevents conventional packet-capture and protocol-parsing tools from directly recovering business data.
A0022-004.description:
A custom transport protocol privatizes protocol headers, handshake flows, field layouts, or encryption algorithms (such as modified TLS handshakes, custom binary frames, or proprietary message encapsulation) so that client-server traffic no longer follows public specs like HTTP/TLS. Even if an attacker captures the traffic with Wireshark or Charles, they see only meaningless binary or encrypted payloads and must reverse-engineer the client's parsing logic before recovering request parameters and response contents.

It is commonly paired with transport protocol encryption (A0022-001) and request data encryption (A0022-002) to cover apps, mini-programs, and client SDKs in non-browser scenarios, materially raising the cost for illicit actors to write automation scripts or launch protocol-level attacks. Because the client must embed the parsing code, the security ultimately depends on whether that logic can be effectively obfuscated and protected against hooking.
A0022-004.limitation: The client-embedded parsing logic can be recovered by attackers via reverse compilation, hooking remote request functions, or dynamic injection tools like Frida; once the algorithm or key is extracted, legitimate packets can be forged at scale and all custom-protocol protection collapses. It is also inapplicable to browser web access, and inconsistent client-server protocol versions cause communication failures, raising maintenance and gray-release cost.
